findings.where: Article specimen: the subhead 'So, what are the key ‘chapter topics’?' compared with the article title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law', at desktop and phone
findings.fault: The subhead uses the same weight and face as the article title, and the same size or larger. At desktop the two are about the same size. At phone width the subhead is clearly bigger than the title (about 46 px line spacing against 37 px). So a section heading inside the article looks more important than the article's own title, and the page shows only one heading level where there should be two.
findings.who_objects: A reader of the article page, who expects the title to be the largest heading and the subheads below it to be smaller. When a subhead outranks the title, the article seems to start again partway down. Angélique would also object: she will add subheads to every article, and this treatment teaches her to use a heading style that competes with the title.

findings.where: Article specimen title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law', at desktop and phone
findings.fault: The apostrophe in 'World's' is the straight typewriter mark, a short vertical tick. Everywhere else the specimen uses curly typographer's quotes: the curly quotation marks in the body and the curly single quotes around ‘chapter topics’ and ‘Abundance’. The largest text on the article page is the one place that gets the cruder mark.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader, and Mark himself, whose look is meant to read as refined and legal-journal grade. A straight apostrophe at title size reads as unfinished typesetting, and it sits right next to correctly set quotes.

findings.where: First screen at phone width: the lockup's second line 'Moseley Infrastructure Advisory Services' beside the reversed mark
findings.fault: The lockup's descriptor wraps, leaving 'Services' alone on a third line. The name-and-logo lockup should read as one fixed unit, but here it breaks the company name across lines wherever the screen happens to cut it.
findings.who_objects: Mark and the founder, for whom 'his name leads, with the logo beside it' is a core test. A lockup that reflows with a one-word last line looks improvised rather than like a set mark.
